chapter_theme: One song at Perungudi (பெருங்குடி) that tells a whole life in a row of verbs, from ten months in the womb to the burning, and asks whether the poet will end this birth that ends in fire.

700.reading: The poet tells a life as people live it: mothers bore them ten months in the womb; they were born, lay, sat, crawled and walked; for a while they embraced fine women and were deluded, carried the burden of the household with their work, settled, declined, died and were burned; he asks whether he will not end this birth that ends in burning. The praise names Mukunda, who in Lanka, with the monkey and his fire and the long sea trembling, came forth, as uncle, the lord of Tamil Vayalur whose fierce hand threw the vel that shook the mountain, at Perungudi of groves, cane and plantain.
700.nuance: The first half is a list of plural past verbs (சமைந்தனர் பிறந்தனர் கிடந்தனர் இருந்தனர் தவழ்ந்தனர் நடந்தனர் ... இறந்தனர்), so the life is everyone's and passes in a breath; only the last line turns to the poet. The household burden (க்ருகபாரம் சுமந்தனர்) is part of the round, not its remedy. The line on Lanka (இலங்கையில் இலங்கிய இலங்களுள் இலங்கு அருள்) plays on the sound இலங்கு and is hard to read.

links.note: Both set marriage and the household inside the march to the burning ground: the Naladiyar mocks the man who sees the corpse carried yet marries and thinks there is joy here, and 700 lists embracing women and bearing the household's burden between crawling and burning.

700 runs a life in plural past verbs, பிறந்தனர் கிடந்தனர் இருந்தனர் தவழ்ந்தனர் நடந்தனர், on to இறந்தனர் and the burning. Naladiyar 29 compresses a death into the report நின்றான் இருந்தான் கிடந்தான் ... சென்றான். Both tell a life as a run of verbs of posture to show how fast it passes; the Naladiyar draws the lesson to do good at once (இன்னினியே), 700 asks to end the birth itself.
